_about: The atlas's music. Each tradition is a way of playing, built in the browser from its scale, voices and manner: an evocation, not a reconstruction. `voices` names who plays it; a voice tied to an `instrument` on the Music shelf (data/music.json) joins only once the viewpoint knows that instrument. `viewpoints` says which tradition a viewpoint hears in which years; `lands` says whose music is heard in a region, for a traveller passing through it. Scales are in cents above the shared tonic, D. A tradition with an `ensemble` is composed: its `tunes` (notes as pitch:beats, / after a phrase, moved by `transpose` semitones onto D) are stated, varied and improvised on by sampled instruments (public/audio, from scripts/fetch_samples.py); one with `recordings` plays those instead. Pieces in data/scores/ are turned into MIDI by scripts/make_midi.py; a MIDI track plays on the ensemble member of its name (role `part` for members heard only there).

traditions.name: The lyre and the aulos
traditions.summary: Greek music, heard through two themes: Mesomedes' Prayer to Calliope and a lullaby from Smyrna. While the years run one carries on, and when time stands still they take turns. traditions.name: Rome and Italy
traditions.summary: The music of the Roman world, heard through two themes from Rome's own surviving songs: the stately Hymn to the Sun that Mesomedes wrote for Hadrian's court, and the Seikilos song, "while you live, shine". While the years run one carries on, and when time stands still they take turns. Each is played as Italy's age would: the lyre and aulos before Rome, the kithara, tibia, water organ and cornu of the empire, the chant and organ of the medieval church, the lutes, viols and harpsichord of the Renaissance, the opera house's strings, mandolin and trumpet, and a modern film orchestra.

tunes.name: Hymn to the Sun · Caravans and monsoons
tunes.about: Rome's ceremonial theme in the medieval church: singers in plain chant, then in organum a fifth apart, then with the organ and bells.
tunes.credit: Transcription on Wikimedia Commons ("Mesomedes Hymn to the Sun.png", Kanjuzi, CC BY-SA 4.0), after Pöhlmann and West.

traditions.name: Chant and consort

Each is played as its age would: the lurs and lyres of the bronze north, the harps and crwths of the Celts, the chant and organ of the medieval church, the lutes, recorders and viols of the Renaissance, the Victorian organ and parlour piano, and a film orchestra.

traditions.name: Maqam
traditions.summary: The modes of Arabic, Persian and Turkish music, heard through two themes Edward Lane noted in Cairo in the 1830s: the chant of a poet of the Hilali epic, and the popular song Doos ya lellee. While the years run one carries on, and when time stands still they take turns. Each is played as its age would: the lyre and reed pipe of Mesopotamia, the barbat, chang and ney of the Sasanian court, the oud, qanun and ney of the golden age, the Ottoman mehter, Cairo's takht with its violin, and a film orchestra. Lane wrote the neutral steps of the maqam as plain notes, and so they are played here.

traditions.name: Raga
traditions.summary: Indian music on the raga, heard through two themes from C. R. Day's book of 1891: a Pillari gita to Ganesha in raga Malahari, the first song a Carnatic student learns, and an old and popular song in raga Bilahari. While the years run one carries on, and when time stands still they take turns. Each is played as its age would, always over the tanpura: voices and veena, the temple's nadaswaram and tavil, the sitar, shehnai and sarangi of the courts, the violin and harmonium of the nineteenth century, and a film orchestra.

traditions.name: The five notes
traditions.summary: Chinese music on the five notes gong, shang, jue, zhi and yu, heard through two themes, the stately Guiding March of the court's processions and the song Mo Li Hua: while the years run one carries on, and when time stands still they take turns. Each is played as its age would: on the xun and bronze bells of the early kingdoms, the qin and xiao of the Han and Tang, the pipa of the Silk Road, the huqin of the teahouse, the suona of the street bands, and the erhu and yangqin of a modern orchestra. As the years pass the tune goes on and the players around it change. Between its verses the qin and the xiao improvise.

tunes.about: China's theme as bronze and clay might have played it: the xun alone, then the se beneath it, then the bell-chime and stone-chime of the Zhou court.
tunes.credit: Barrow's melody as set on Wikimedia Commons ("Jasmine barrow.svg", public domain); arranged for this atlas.

tunes.about: China's theme for the Han and the Tang: the scholar's qin, the xiao singing over it, then the court's se and bells.

tunes.about: China's theme in the age of the Silk Road: the pipa from Central Asia, trembling its long notes, with the di, the sheng's chords and a frame drum.

tunes.name: Guan Ju (The Ospreys)
tunes.about: The first ode of the Book of Songs, sung at the Zhou court: "Guan guan cry the ospreys, on the islet in the river." One note to each syllable, as a hand wrote it above a 1768 printing of the Wei family's Ming court songs; played slowly on the xun, then sung over the se, then with bronze bells and stone chimes.
tunes.credit: Transcribed for this atlas from the scan on Wikimedia Commons ("Guanju of GISHI GAKUFU 1768.jpg", Kato Toru, CC0); data/scores/guanju.json.

tunes.name: Sacrificial Hymn to Confucius
tunes.about: The hymn of the Confucian temple, in six stanzas, one note to each syllable, as fixed in 1743 and printed by Van Aalst in 1884, played as he describes: the bell-chime gives each note, the zithers answer, flutes, sheng and six singers take it up, and the stone-chime closes it. Its manner, though not this melody, is that of the ancient ritual music, yayue.
tunes.credit: Transcribed for this atlas from Van Aalst's staff and gongche notation (data/scores/confucius-hymn.json).

tunes.name: Madame Wang
tunes.about: A popular song of Peking: a lovesick girl fends off her neighbour's remedies, verse after verse. Played as in a teahouse, on pipa, huqin and di, with clapper and wood block.
tunes.credit: Transcribed for this atlas from Van Aalst's staff (data/scores/madame-wang.json).

tunes.name: Ma-ma hao ming-pai (Oh Mamma, You Understand Me Well)
tunes.about: An air Van Aalst found "exceedingly popular in North China" in the 1880s, set as a twentieth-century Chinese orchestra might: the erhu sings it over the yangqin and strings, the di takes it up, and the whole orchestra plays it home.
tunes.credit: Transcribed for this atlas from Van Aalst's staff (data/scores/mama-hao-mingbai.json).

traditions.name: Yō and in
traditions.summary: Japanese music on the yō and in scales, heard through two themes: Taki's solemn Kōjō no Tsuki, "the moon over the ruined castle", and the folk song Sakura. While the years run one carries on, and when time stands still they take turns. Each is played as Japan's age would: clay flutes and the wagon zither, the gagaku of the Heian court with its shō, hichiriki and ryūteki, the koto, shakuhachi and shamisen of Edo, Meiji's harmonium and school choirs, and a film orchestra.

traditions.name: Gamelan
traditions.summary: The gamelan of Java and its neighbours, heard through two themes composed for this atlas in its styles, since its music was passed on by ear rather than written: a court ladrang in pelog and a children's song in slendro. While the years run one carries on, and when time stands still they take turns. Each is played as its age would: the Dong Son bronze drums and bamboo, the first bronze keys, the gamelan of Borobudur's age, the full court gamelan with its gongs marking each cycle, keroncong, and a film orchestra.

traditions.name: Panpipes of the Andes
traditions.summary: The music of the Andes, heard through two themes: Hanacpachap cussicuinin, the Quechua hymn printed in Lima in 1631, and a huayno. While the years run one carries on, and when time stands still they take turns. Each is played as its age would: clay ocarinas and the conch, antara and siku panpipes, quena flutes and the great bombo, the voices, organ and harp of the colonial church, the harp, violin and charango, and a film orchestra.

traditions.name: Mbira
traditions.summary: The mbira music of the Shona and their neighbours, heard through two themes composed for this atlas in its styles, since it was passed on by ear rather than written: a ceremonial mbira cycle and a call-and-response song. While the years run one carries on, and when time stands still they take turns. Each is played as its age would: voices, clapping and the kudu horn, the karimba, the interlocking mbira of Great Zimbabwe and the Mutapa court with hosho and ngoma, the xylophones of the south, and a modern band.
